gaps.text: In-line measurement of Melt temperature at the measurement point with temperature sensor (melt thermocouple or probe sensor)

Combining several spectroscopy methods (data fusion) (Fusion level: one model per method first, then joined or block-scaled variables, compared against the best single method. Both methods must look at the same melt volume at a common time step, ideally with a combined ATR plus Raman probe head, and each block keeps its own calibration and diagnostics. The fused model must beat the best single-method model on held-out runs, otherwise the second instrument is dropped.)
No supplied source states probe, crystal or fiber temperature ratings, so a maximum melt temperature for the probe cannot be given.
No supplied source describes cleaning or anti-fouling measures for a hot polymer melt interface.

items.finding: High-level data fusion first fits supervised models to each data matrix.
items.how_it_applies: This supports starting with one model per method before any joined or block-scaled variables, as the gap proposes.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The review is general and not specific to hot polymer melt, API, ATR or Raman, so the sequence may need local validation.

citation.quote: The high-level data fusion (HLDF) (also called "decision-level" fusion) works on a decision level. This means that the first step is to fit some supervised models to each data matrix.
citation.label: E02 ¶33

items.finding: Instrument complementarity alone was not sufficient to improve prediction of several CQAs in a Raman and FT-IR food study.
items.how_it_applies: This cautions that a fused ATR plus Raman model must be compared against the best single method on held-out runs, and dropped if it does not improve.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The cited study is food analytical, not a hot polymer/API melt, and uses Raman and FT-IR rather than necessarily the same probe configuration.

citation.quote: In some situations, instrument complementarity (not data complementarity) was not sufficient to improve the performance of predictive several CQAs, as shown by a Raman and FT-IR data based food analytical study [73].
citation.label: E02 ¶36

items.finding: Epoxy resins adhered firmly to a zinc-selenide ATR crystal, and removing them damaged the fragile crystal even with great care.
items.how_it_applies: This suggests testing how the hot polymer/API melt interacts with the ATR crystal and whether cleaning or anti-fouling can remove build-up without damaging the crystal.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The work used epoxy resins on ZnSe in a laboratory ATR study, not a hot polymer melt with API, so adhesion and damage may differ.

citation.quote: The first of these inaccuracies arose from the fact that most of the ATR work was carried out using epoxy resins on a zinc-selenide crystal. These resins firmly adhere to their substrate, and thus, even exercising the greatest of care, when removed, damage was sustained to the rather fragile crystal.
citation.label: E04 ¶690
